# GLRMask

<!-- Generated by scripts/sync-guide.py from docs/content. Do not edit this output. -->

GLRMask is a grammar-constrained decoding library for high-throughput LLM serving. It is optimized for fast mask computation with extremely low tail latency, even for complex grammars.

GLRMask supports general context-free grammars, including ambiguous ones. It accepts JSON Schema, Lark, and GLRMask's native format: GLRM.

[Website](https://glrmask.com) · [Paper](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23273556)

#### Dynamic mode

GLRMask’s dynamic mode trades some mask-generation speed for lower cold-start latency. It is heavily based on [llguidance](https://github.com/guidance-ai/llguidance).

</picture>

[Explore Dynamic JSON results](https://glrmask.com/?dataset=json&mode=dynamic#benchmarks).

There was no CPU pinning or SMT sibling reservation, and checkpoint publication overlapped the benchmark. Saved telemetry cannot isolate scheduling effects; latency stabilization is not certified. Successful builds do not establish semantic correctness. All 9,558 JSON schemas were attempted: build errors are Dynamic 232, Balanced 232, Static 233 and llguidance 1,226. Incorrect examples are 460 for each GLRMask mode and 100 for llguidance; runtime-error examples are 0 and 6 respectively. JavaScript attempts all 55 fixtures: all builds succeed, with 1 incorrect example per GLRMask mode and 4 for llguidance. Headline TBM excludes incomplete or nonaccepted valid trajectories; all outcomes remain in the raw records. This finite corpus does not establish full-language equivalence or whole-corpus dominance.

[Native AWS benchmark details](docs/benchmark-aws-2026-10-14.md). Historical [October 8 Mac JSON](docs/benchmark-cfa-2026-10-08.md) and [October 9 Mac JavaScript](docs/benchmark-javascript-2026-10-09.md) reports are retained with their original measurement protocols. These are source builds, not measurements of the published 0.2 packages.

## Getting started

### Installation

#### Python

```bash
python -m pip install glrmask
```

#### Rust

```bash
cargo add glrmask
```

#### Native C++ and Node.js

Native bindings are available for C++ and JavaScript/TypeScript on Node.js. The [C++ guide and C API](https://glrmask.com/api/cpp/) and [JavaScript and TypeScript guide](https://glrmask.com/api/javascript/) cover source builds, platform artifacts, ownership, composition, and the complete supported API. The Node.js addon runs the Rust engine directly; browser WebAssembly is a separate target.

### Usage

GLRMask has four core types:

- `Grammar`: the source-language definition, without compilation settings.
- `Module`: a reusable, independently configured grammar with bindings and any retained compilation work. It may still have unresolved externs.
- `Constraint`: a fully runnable grammar compiled against a specific vocabulary.
- `ConstraintState`: the mutable state for a single generated sequence.

**Source API status:** `Module` and `Expr` are unreleased. Published 0.3.1 packages
use `PreparedGrammar` for reusable preparation. The decoding quickstarts below
work with that release; the new assembly APIs require a matching source build.

Use direct `Grammar.compile` for a closed source, or a `Module` when local
settings, late-bound children, or retained work are needed. `Expr.choice` and
`Expr.sequence` group grammar leaves without adding an extra lexer scope at each
operator. See [modules and expressions](https://github.com/IsaacBreen/glrmask/blob/main/docs/module-api.md)
for construction, open precompilation, and persistence examples.

### Python quickstart

```python
import glrmask

vocab = glrmask.Vocab.from_id_to_bytes({0: b"hello", 1: b" ", 2: b"world"})
grammar = glrmask.Grammar.from_ebnf('start ::= "hello" " " "world"')
constraint = grammar.compile(vocab)
state = constraint.start()
for token_id, expected in [(0, [True, False, False]),
                           (1, [False, True, False]),
                           (2, [False, False, True])]:
    assert state.mask().tolist() == expected
    state.commit_token(token_id)
assert state.is_accepting()
```

Python masks are NumPy Boolean arrays indexed by original model token ID.

The next compatibility release targets ordinary, GIL-enabled CPython 3.9
through 3.15. Its `cp39-abi3` wheels use Python's stable extension ABI, so one
wheel per operating-system/architecture combination can serve multiple Python
versions. This does not imply support for free-threaded Python (`cp314t`,
`cp315t` or `abi3t`): the extension explicitly retains the GIL requirement.

The expanded build matrix covers Windows x64/ARM64, macOS Intel/Apple Silicon,
and Linux x64/ARM64 with either glibc or musl. Linux glibc Python wheels retain
the manylinux2014 baseline; native C++/Node binaries use glibc 2.28 or newer.
See [the compatibility guide](https://github.com/IsaacBreen/glrmask/blob/main/docs/compatibility.md)
for runtime requirements and the distinction between source support and
published package availability.

### Rust quickstart

```rust
use glrmask::{Grammar, Vocab};

fn main() -> glrmask::Result<()> {
    let vocab = Vocab::new(vec![
        (0, b"hello".to_vec()), (1, b" ".to_vec()), (2, b"world".to_vec()),
    ]);
    let grammar = Grammar::from_ebnf(r#"start ::= "hello" " " "world""#);
    let constraint = grammar.compile(&vocab)?;
    let mut state = constraint.start();
    for (token_id, expected) in [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 4)] {
        assert_eq!(state.mask()[0] & 7, expected);
        state.commit_token(token_id)?;
    }
    assert!(state.is_accepting());
    Ok(())
}
```

Rust masks are packed `u32` bitsets. Bit `token_id % 32` of word `token_id / 32` indicates whether that token is allowed.

### Composition and reusable grammars

Use `extern token NAME` for a one-event exact-token contract and
`extern grammar NAME` for a general byte/event grammar fragment. Bind source
children to `Grammar`, or cold and independently precompiled children to `Module`.
Neither child needs to be complete before attachment. Modules keep their own
local compilation settings; `Grammar` does not store those settings:

```rust
use glrmask::{Grammar, Module, Result, Vocab};

# fn demo(vocab: &Vocab, marker: u32) -> Result<()> {
let mut child = Module::new(&Grammar::from_glrm(
    r#"extern token MARK start body nt body = "item" MARK"#,
));
child.precompile(vocab)?;
let mut parent = Module::new(&Grammar::from_glrm(
    "extern grammar ITEM start root nt root = ITEM",
));
parent.precompile(vocab)?;
parent.bind("ITEM", &child)?;
parent.bind("ITEM::MARK", glrmask::Token::new(marker))?;
let constraint = parent.compile(vocab)?;
# let _ = constraint;
# Ok(())
# }
```

Binding mutates the receiving handle atomically. `clone()` makes an independently
editable handle sharing immutable internals. Children are captured as snapshots;
editing the original child later does not change existing parents. Repeated
references to one inline grammar share bindings, while separately attached
occurrences can be specialized independently.
`unbound()` exposes outstanding typed paths such as `ITEM::MARK`; `externs()` also
includes bound declarations. Final compilation requires every declared parameter
to be resolved. `Module.save()` and `Module.load()` preserve source, settings,
open bindings and retained work with the same vocabulary identity. Vocabulary
is supplied to root compilation operations, not every cold child constructor.

Exact token sets and compact ranges consume one original ID, never its decoded
spelling. A JSON Schema is an ordinary grammar-valued child. Exact event values
can also bind directly to grammar slots; `Grammar::exact` constructs a standalone
event-set grammar when needed. See the [full guide](GUIDE.md),
[native syntax](docs/glrm-format.md), and [exact-token ranges](docs/exact-token-ranges.md).

`Expr.choice` and `Expr.sequence` combine whole grammar or module leaves without
adding scopes at intermediate grouping operators. The leaves retain independent
bindings, options and any retained work. Use `Grammar.from_expr` for source-only
expressions, and `Module::from_expr` (Rust) or `Module(expr)` (Python) for
configured expressions. See [module lifecycle](docs/module-lifecycle.md).

### Choosing an optimization mode

`FastBuild` favors short cold starts using ordinary Dynamic, `Balanced` uses the
native middle-ground configuration, and `FastRuntime` favors mask-generation speed.
`Auto` is the default. Python exposes the corresponding uppercase names. These are
implementation trade-offs, not different language semantics.
Each Module captures its own `ModuleOptions`. A raw child uses default options,
not its parent's overrides. Unsupported combinations of retained representations
produce an error instead of silently rebuilding or discarding supplied work.

```rust
# use glrmask::{BuildOptions, Grammar, Optimization, Result, Vocab};
# fn demo(grammar: &Grammar<'_>, vocab: &Vocab) -> Result<()> {
let constraint = grammar.compile_with(
    vocab,
    BuildOptions::default().optimization(Optimization::FastBuild),
)?;
# let _ = constraint;
# Ok(())
# }
```

### Completion and forcing

Set `end_tokens` on the final compile call. `is_accepting()` means the
current output is a complete match, possibly with valid continuations. Commit the
sampled end token before stopping. An initially accepting grammar can instead stop
immediately if that is the application's policy.

The read-only `forced_tokens()` query returns a safe library-canonical prefix of
genuinely forced ordinary text. It uses the longest admitted nonempty spelling
and lowest-ID alias, retains exact-event IDs, and stops at root acceptance or an
event boundary that greedy text would cross. The correctness-first reference may
construct full masks and reports typed resource failures as errors. This is one
canonical sequence, not an exhaustive tree of equivalent original-ID histories.
Raw-byte `commit_bytes()` remains separate. See [the forcing contract](docs/forcing.md).

### Source formats

Native GLRM has optional semicolons, `grammar NAME { ... }`, explicit `t`/`nt`
declarations, typed externs, scoped ignore, Unicode/byte expressions and regular
intersection/subtraction. Native `shortest { ... }` syntax is removed; the internal
prefix-minimal operation and Lark's regular-body `[lazy]` remain. Native source contains no numeric-token, special-token-name or
inline JSON literals. Lark accepts those selected compatibility forms only in its
explicit `llm` profile. Unsupported priorities, capture/sampling annotations,
substring generation and regex-internal lazy quantifiers are errors.

## How it works

GLRMask maintains a GLR parser state for the generated prefix. A precomputed deterministic weighted automaton computes the next-token mask by reading each parser stack, intersecting Boolean vocabulary masks along each traversal and unioning alternative paths.

See [How it works](https://glrmask.com/implementation/) for the explanation and diagrams.
